newsitem.title: ANGOLA: ANGOLA'S UNITA CHILD SOLDIERS BEGIN TREK HOME.
newsitem.headline: ANGOLA'S UNITA CHILD SOLDIERS BEGIN TREK HOME.

text.p: The first 499 child soldiers of Angola's former guerrilla movement UNITA are homebound at last from a camp where they have been disarmed together with 5,000 other former rebels.

There are an estimated 7,000 boy soldiers, aged from as young as 11 up to 18, in camps across Angola where about 62,000 UNITA soldiers have been disarmed since January as part of a peace process ending two decades of war.
Ten large trucks at Vila Nova camp, the first assembly area to be opened last year, stood ready to transport the young soldiers to their villages from Wednesday.
Each boy will carry a kit of food, clothing and tools weighing 300 kg and will be dropped off at posts close to their villages. They will also receive $180 to restart their lives.

The U.N. special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, handed the first eight boys their demobilisation cards at a ceremony on Tuesday to kickstart the programme before the first summer rains fall and make roads impassable.
A total of 100,000 soldiers from the government and UNITA are to be demobilised under a 1994 pact that has brought peace to the still divided country.

Jose Abel, 16, the second child soldier to be handed his card, said he was wounded in battle with soldiers loyal to the government of Eduardo dos Santos whose MPLA party was UNITA's foe since the end of Portuguese rule.
"I am very pleased to be going home. I joined UNITA in 1993 but was shot in the leg and wounded during fighting in Huila Province. I then went to hospital," he told Reuters.
Martins Candimba, 18, the first to receive his demobilisation card, said: "I want to go home to my father and study. I have been in the military for four years."
Fautinho Muteka, the Angolan government's peace negotiator in a joint ceasefire commission, told UNITA troops the war was over and it was a good idea to go home.

"Everything has been put in place so you can go home because the war is over. Now everyone should choose where they want to live. To go back is a good idea," Muteka said from a home made mud and grass podium.
"Now that the war is finished we have to reconcile and build the country and make it possible for everyone to contribute so everyone can eat and be clothed," he said to cheers.
UNITA Brigadier Eliope Ekolelo labelled the start of demobilisation a "decisive element for peace".
Carlo Scaramello of the U.N. aid coordination agency UNCAH told Reuters the child soldiers would be demobilised from the 15 assembly camps over the next five weeks.
A total of 186 child soldiers from the Angolan Armed Forces would also be demobilised under the programme.
"The first phase is very important because it will show us if the system is viable. It will be a test and a way of enforcing free circulation of people," Scaramello said.
The British-based Save the Children Fund has helped to trace the families of some of the youths being demobilised.
"Most of the families we have located knew where their children were," said the Fund's Claire Moberly.
"In other cases many have not seen their children for five years and they can't wait for them to come home."
